Peak Poker Performance

      As the deadline for any task gets pushed further into the fu-
      ture, delay increases and our motivation to tackle the task de-
      creases. Impulsiveness multiples the effects of delay, and so
      impulsive people feel the effects of time far less acutely.

    Impulsive people generally wait until the last possible moment to start
their tasks and are more likely to succumb to temptations along the way.
    Steel’s work is very interesting because he showed that procrastina-
tors make the same plans to get to work as non-procrastinators, but they
differ in the way they take action. They start off with good intentions, but
those are not enough to get them to do what they need to do. The trick is
to close the intention-action gap; there are many ways to do that. Tweak
any one of the four variables in the formula and you can change your level
of procrastination. We’ll get back to the idea of tweaks in just a bit, but
first I want to explain the deeper emotions behind why we procrastinate.

Types of Procrastinators
Psychologists have recently become more interested in the deeper emo-
tional reasons behind why we procrastinate and looking at the underlying
emotions behind most such instances. This reveals that most cases of pro-
crastination are an attempt to cope with our emotions, as fear is a main
driver of procrastination. Some people have a fear of success; others a fear
of failure. We may even feel panic when we set impossibly high goals.
    Anger is at the root of some procrastination. If we believe that some-
one is trying to control us, we might rebel by not doing what we are “sup-
posed” to be doing. A strong dislike for the task at hand is another driver
of procrastination, as is depression. If you are suffering from depression,
it can definitely slow you down. Finally, seeking pleasure is another de-
structive driver. When we attempt to seek pleasure and avoid pain, pro-
crastination is a probable outcome.
    It is generally accepted that there are two types of procrastinators:
the tense type and the relaxed type. The tense type feels an immense
pressure to succeed, which can exacerbate a fear of failure. The relaxed
type blows off work that he or she doesn’t like by playing or socializing.

                                                 Beating Procrastination

Studies show that relaxed, pleasure-seeking procrastinators are prone to
being easily frustrated and reluctant to set goals that are deemed to be
too challenging, painful, or dull.
    Neil Fiore (2007) goes further by describing a tense–afraid type of
procrastinator who feels overwhelmed by perfectionist demands and
pressures, uncertain about goals, unrealistic about time, indecisive, and
often unconfident. The root problem for the tense–afraid procrastinator
is that they feel their worth is determined by what they do. Therefore,
failing is terrifying. There are other subtypes of the tense–afraid procras-
tinator – there’s the one who is afraid of success because if they succeed,
continued success will be expected. And there is a type who needs to feel
in control and/or resist control by someone else.

Self-Verification Theory of Procrastination
According to William Swann, people want to be known and understood by
others according to their own firmly held beliefs and feelings about them-
selves. This is known as self-verification and it can drive procrastination.
Let me explain.
   Suppose I see myself as a smart, successful student. Self-verification
theory says that I will want people to see me that way as well: I want the
way they see me to match up with my own beliefs about myself. Because
I have a vested interest in this state of congruence, I’ll do everything in
my power to maintain it – including procrastinate. If I’m worried that I
might fail at some new task and therefore wreck my image, I’ll be moti-
vated to procrastinate. I have always been good at school but what if I’m
bad at business? If others think I’m good, smart, and capable, I want their
vision of me to be maintained.
   Notice that the opposite is also true. If people tend to think I’m lazy
and stupid, self-verification theory says that I’ll match my behaviors with
that, too. There seems to be a basic fundamental need for our behaviors
and identities to match up. According to author Mark Manson, the more a
task threatens to change how you view yourself, how you believe your-
self to be, the more you’ll procrastinate on it. The self-verification proc-

Peak Poker Performance

ess essentially creates resistance. Any time a new goal threatens the
viewpoint you hold of yourself, the more you’ll procrastinate. There are
other ways to resist, including self-handicapping, a cognitive strategy
used to preserve self-esteem; we are especially likely to use it when we
fear failure. For example, if we want to be seen as smart, we’ll often put
off things because then we can attribute our failure to not having enough
time. This is very different than taking plenty of time to finish something
and failing. In that case, the fault would lie squarely on us.
   Another means of resistance is something called active avoidance,
where you do things that make you look busy, but they are not really im-
portant. For example, you may spend a ton of time planning out all the
books and videos you want to study to improve your game, but that
doesn’t move you towards actually doing the work of improving your
game. At some point, you have to stop planning and get to work.
   Planning and coming up with systems and processes is very important
but we should be able to put together our action plan relatively quickly. If
we spend too much time researching and dreaming, we will effectively
end up spinning our wheels and not making any progress. Planning only
looks like progress because we are in motion, but we aren’t really getting
very far. You have to actually do the thing that will make a difference.
   To figure out if you are relying on self-verification, ask yourself
whether your life will be better if you make the change you are procrasti-
nating on. We often self-sabotage because we don’t think our life will be
better if we make the changes, but this is an unconscious belief. To find
out if you are harboring any self-limiting, self-sabotaging beliefs:

   ♠ Think about a goal or change that you have been procrastinating
       on and write it down.
   ♠ Think about whether your life will be better if you make this
       change or achieve this goal.
   ♠ Write out a list of all the ways your life will be worse if you make
       the change. These are the stories you are telling yourself that are
       holding you back.

                                                  Beating Procrastination

   ♠ Write out a list of all the ways your life will be better if you make
       the change.
   ♠ Analyze your lists and see if you are harboring any self-limiting
       beliefs. Are you trying to hold on to any underlying beliefs?


    This exercise sounds easy on the surface, but you have to dig in to un-
cover the deep, underlying reasons you are self-sabotaging. To recap,
common limiting beliefs include fear of failure, fear of success, and fear of
disappointing someone. If you uncover these, you can make an effort to
shift your identity. Also, work to come up with strategies to address any
of the ways your life will be worse when you make changes. Suppose you
want to lose a few pounds. You might believe that you’ll have to give up
all of your favorite foods, which will be no fun. Try to come up with some
strategies for enjoying your favorites by eating limited or controlled por-
tions. The goal is to keep everything in balance.
    The bottom line is that if you want to change how you act, you have to
change what you believe about yourself. This is hard work and takes time
and effort. We are often very wedded to our beliefs about ourselves. If
you are engaging in procrastination for self-verification reasons, you
probably would like to “cure” yourself with a quick strategy. There is a
deeper level reason for procrastination caused by emotional resistance,
for which there is no simple cure. It will take a bit more digging and effort
to rid yourself of this type of procrastination.
    While chronic, deep-rooted procrastination takes a lot of effort to
eradicate, there are a number of strategies and tactics that you can try
out to short-circuit run of the mill procrastination.

Tactics To Fight Procrastination

Don’t Wait Until You Feel Like It: Just Get Started
One of the biggest misconceptions about motivation is that we have to
feel inspired to get started on an aversive task. You may not feel like put-
ting in the volume you need to, but that doesn’t have to stop you from

Peak Poker Performance

getting started. We know that attitudes follow behavior at least as much
as behaviors follow attitudes, so if we just get started on something we
don’t feel like doing, we will often get motivated. Usually getting started
is the hardest part – once we do, motivation follows.
    Getting started is a key strategy if you find yourself procrastinating.
Don’t think about finishing the job; that can be overwhelming. Just focus
on getting started. Taking the first step is all you need to do. Once you
get started, you’ll often see that a task isn’t as bad as you thought it
would be. As long as you have just enough motivation to get started,
that’s all you need, as Dr. Pychyl (2010) observed,

      When you find yourself thinking things like “I’ll feel more like
      doing this tomorrow,” “I work better under pressure,” “There’s
      lots of time left,” “I can do this in a few hours tonight,” let that
      be a flag or signal or stimulus to indicate that you are about to
      needlessly delay the task, and let it also be the stimulus to just
      get started.

    Tal Ben-Shahar shares a concept called the five minute takeoff in his
book Choose the Life You Want (2012). If we know that we are going to
have to be on task for five minutes, it can help lower our resistance.
Regularly dedicating small amounts of time to an onerous task can help us
make significant progress. Get started on whatever you’ve been avoiding
and try to stick with it for five minutes. You can always add additional five
minute segments until you build up to a meaningful time frame. Plus,
limiting the time you have to spend on a task makes it more fun, less
frustrating, more structured, and less difficult because you can see the
light at the end of the tunnel.
    The important thing to remember is to just get started. Start any-
where! Don’t worry about the whole task and don’t concern yourself with
whether or not you get it finished. Pychyl says that we make things out to
be a bigger deal than they actually are. Taking small steps helps us to get
over that illusory thought process.

                                                     Beating Procrastination

Use Implementation Intentions
The best way to get into action is by using if-then planning, also known as
an implementation intention. Peter Gollwitzer, a psychology professor at
New York University, is the leading proponent of this technique and he
suggests that setting goals and even writing them down has a relatively
weak effect on behavior. Instead we should focus on tools that get us
into what he calls “goal striving” mode. There is a huge difference be-
tween setting a goal and making a plan for exactly when, where, and how
you will behave to reach your goal. He calls the plan an implementation
intention. To use it, you state explicitly what behavior you will do, and
when and where you will do it. The “if” part of your statement describes
the stimulus for action and the “then” portion describes the action you will
take. Let me give you an example.
   A study was conducted in Germany where two groups of people were
asked to write an essay about how they spent Christmas Eve and then
send it to the researchers within 48 hours. The first group was given the
assignment and no additional instructions. The second group was given
the assignment and asked to make a specific plan about when, where, and
how they were going to fulfill the assignment. Only 24% of the first group
sent in their essays, while 68% of the implementation intention group re-
turned theirs! That’s a very strong result to say the least. In fact, it is fairly
uncommon in psychology to see such a strong effect. Many more follow-
up studies have been conducted, which show much the same pattern. Im-
plementation intentions work by getting us to come up with clear strate-
gies for how we will accomplish certain tasks. They can be used to help us
exercise more, eat right, do our homework, or even meditate more often.
   Here are a few more ideas from Gollwitzer’s work that I think you’ll
find useful:

    ♠ Goal specificity is very important. State explicitly what you intend
        to accomplish (e.g. write 10 hand history reviews versus some
        hand history reviews).

Peak Poker Performance

   ♠ Getting started is the hardest part of goal setting if what you need
       to do is overwhelming or unpleasant. Use implementation
       intentions to specify how and when you’ll get started.
   ♠ Find ways to deal with distractions and disruptions. If you get off
       track, make an implementation intention to get back on.
   ♠ If your plan stops working, make a new one.
   ♠ You have got to be committed to your goals for implementation
       intentions to be effective.
   ♠ Consider what gets in the way of you reaching your goals and
       make plans to deal with those obstacles.
   ♠ Write out your implementation intention plans and keep them
       where you can see them; for example, “As soon as I finish
       breakfast, I will exercise for 10 minutes.”
   ♠ Implementation intentions provide structure to ambiguous tasks
       because it makes them more concrete. Research shows we are
       much less likely to procrastinate on concrete tasks.

   The reason that Gollwitzer’s strategy works so well is that it is a form
of pre-decision. We pre-decide that we are going to do something and
then as we repeat the behavior it becomes a habit. Our brain becomes
wired for that activity and it no longer requires willpower.

Goals are Super Fuel for Motivation
As you can probably discern from the work of Gollwitzer and Steel, pow-
erful goals provide us with motivation. Human beings are teleological: we
are focused on future outcomes. We operate best when we have a target
to aim at. Motivation tends to be highest when we are aiming at a clear
target. Do you have clear goals or are you aimless?
   For best results, your goals should be challenging, meaningful, specific,
and feasible. We want to stretch ourselves, but not so far that we snap!
Also, it’s important that our goals be intrinsically valuable so we are inter-
nally motivated to achieve them.

                                                   Beating Procrastination

    If your goal is very long term, it is best to decrease delay by breaking it
into mini-goals. Then work backward to transform your overall mission
into daily and weekly goals. This helps you get into a routine of working
towards your goals. What can you do every single day to accomplish your
overall goal? Predictability is your friend!
    Another thing to consider is that you want to focus on behaviors and
not results. This is very important in a game like poker where our results are
not under our immediate control. Scores of studies show that only setting
results goals is de-motivating. We can increase our motivation (and reduce
procrastination) by focusing on the process of getting to what we want.
The focus of every hand should not be the result, but how well you played
it. Focus on the process of playing each hand as well as you possibly can.
Measure your success by how much effort you are putting in.

Gamify Aversive Tasks
The easiest way to make unpleasant tasks more pleasant is to turn them
into a game. Take a look at what it is about the task you are procrastinat-
ing on that is so unappealing to you. Your mission is to see how you can
reduce the unpleasantness of the task – even if it is only by a small
amount.
   Dr. Pychyl (2010) gave the example of a cleaning, which many people
find boring and frustrating:

      You look at it and assess it and say, “Oh, this is so boring and I
      find it so frustrating”, so you make a little game out of it. How
      can you make it interesting? So I might play a game of, “How
      many of these clothes could I get put away in 20 minutes?”
      And you find something to do – some competition within it,
      and so all of a sudden you make it interesting, and much less
      boring and frustrating in the process.
